Pick and Place Objects in a Cluttered Scene Using Deep Reinforcement Learning

  • September 2020
  • International Journal of Mechanical & Mechatronics Engineering 20(4):50-57
Authors:
Marwan Mohammed
  • Abertay University
L.C. Kwek
  • Multimedia University

Abstract and Figures

This paper presents a robotic grasp-to-place system that has the capability of grasping objects in sparse and cluttered environments. The key feature of the system is that it handles both primitive actions of picking and placing of objects with an explicit framework using raw RGB-D images. Thus, the contribution of this paper is to model such a complete manipulation system with reasonable computational complexity. To achieve this, the camera captured RGB images of the scene, and 3d point cloud information are used to generate heightmaps at the robot grasp-workspace. The heightmap is rotated by 36 different angles before feeding into the network in order to generate a set of 36 pixel-wise Q-value maps, which is then passed into a Dense Network (DenseNet) to generate predictions of Q-values. Q-values are a measure of future expected reward in the formula of Q-learning from reinforcement learning. This effectively gives us values for predictions for 36 different grasping angles for every visible location in the robot grasp-workspace. In the simulation, exhaustive experimental results demonstrate that our framework successfully grasp objects with a grasp success rate and grasp efficiency, at almost 80~95% for both. As for place task, our framework successfully placed objects with a place success rate to at least 90 % through all test-cases. Index Term-Robotic grasp-to-place system, pixel-wise Q-value, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Q-learning, DenseNet.

Pick and Place Objects in a Cluttered Scene Using
Deep Reinforcement Learning
Marwan Qaid Mohammed, Kwek Lee Chung, Chua Shing Chyi
Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Multimedia University (MMU), 75450, Melaka, Malaysia.
E-mails: marwan.qaid.mohammed@gmail.com [ORCID: 0000-0001-9734-6267], lckwek@mmu.edu.my ,
scchua@mmu.edu.my
Abstract— This paper presents a robotic grasp-to-place
system that has the capability of grasping objects in sparse and
cluttered environments. The key feature of the system is that it
handles both primitive actions of picking and placing of objects
with an explicit framework using raw RGB-D images. Thus,
the contribution of this paper is to model such a complete
manipulation system with reasonable computational
complexity. To achieve this, the camera captured RGB images
of the scene, and 3d point cloud information are used to
generate heightmaps at the robot grasp-workspace. The
heightmap is rotated by 36 different angles before feeding into
the network in order to generate a set of 36 pixel-wise Q-value
maps, which is then passed into a Dense Network (DenseNet) to
generate predictions of Q-values. Q-values are a measure of
future expected reward in the formula of Q-learning from
reinforcement learning. This effectively gives us values for
predictions for 36 different grasping angles for every visible
location in the robot grasp-workspace. In the simulation,
exhaustive experimental results demonstrate that our
framework successfully grasp objects with a grasp success rate
and grasp efficiency, at almost 80~95% for both. As for place
task, our framework successfully placed objects with a place
success rate to at least 90 % through all test-cases.
Index Term— Robotic grasp-to-place system, pixel-wise Q-
value, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Q-learning,
DenseNet.
I. INTRODUCTION
Robots are found everywhere, particularly in production
lines where robots are extensively used due to demanding of
increasing both production speed and consistency. Robotic
grasping is one of the common mechanisms that have wide
application scenarios in industrial applications [1] such as
grasping small objects lying on flat surfaces [2][3], grasping
deformable objects [4] and so on. Grasping comprises an
action of gripping and moving an object from one place to
another. Thus, Robotic manipulation, despite its long
history, remains a challenging problem [5]. The interaction
between a robot and its environment requires perception
about the environment, which helps the robot in taking a
clear decision about the object type and its location.
Robotic grasping has been intensively categorized by
many researches, into relatively two categories. The first
category is analytic methods [6], which considers the
performance based on modeling contact forces and their
ability of resistance to external wrenches [7][8], or their
capability to constrain object movability during grasping [9].
Whereas, the second category is data-driven methods[10],
which mainly depends on machine learning for developing
models that map sensor readings to human labels [11] or
physical trials [12].
Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is used in
various robotic applications[13] such as placement [14],
grasping deformable object [15], grasping in cluttered scene
[16]. Meanwhile, DRL has led to advance technology by
using visual and tactile features, particularly in robotic
grasping [5]. Besides, DRL has brought tremendous
solutions for difficult tasks, which are difficult to be
automatically executed and repeated, using end-to-end
training [17] based on trial-and-error [18][19]. To this end,
DRL-based robotic grasping, despite its beneficial sides,
remains a challenging problem, not only in building an
interpretative model framework but also in terms of the
complexity of needed resources. Using a big dataset [20]
(e.g. graspable regions in RGB-D images [21], point clouds
[20][22]–[25]), requires a high capacity of memory with a
high graphics processor unit (GPU) such as NVidia Drivers,
which is one of the biggest challenges in DRL today. In this
project, we propose an explicit pick-to-place framework
that can be less complex as compared to others [26]–[28],
and can also be trained using reasonable CPU-Memory or
GPU-Memory, while taking into consideration training time
and adequate data for sufficient evaluation analysis.
In our proposed framework, we have used
convolutional neural network (CNN) to compute the Q-
value map for grasping action. The fully convolutional
network (FCN) is used to model the Q-value function for
grasping. Each entry , which indicates the pixel of the
heightmap image representation of the state  , in the Q-
value map corresponds to some 3D location in the
workspace, whereas the predicted Q-value at 
represents the expected future reward of executing grasping
action . The pixel and corresponding actions with the
heights Q-value prediction is passed to the controller which
executes the grasping. Then, if the robot has successfully
grasped the object, the robot will place the object into the
pre-defined place-workspace.
In this paper, we aim to come out with a complete
manipulation system (reaching-to-grasping-to-placing),
which is jointly trained based on end-to-end learning. We
attempt to avoid complex model architecture so that
moderate GPU or CPU features would be sufficient for
training purposes. Related works are presented in Section 2,
whereas Section 3 presents the methodology of our proposed
framework with details of training and testing specifications.
The result and discussion are presented in Section 4. Lastly,
we conclude our work as stated in Section 5.
II. RELATED WORK
There are many studies concentrating on grasping or
grasp pose detection such as segmenting the target object
[27][29], learning eye-hand coordination [24], template-
based approach with the convex hull [30][25] or using a
bounding box [23], and detecting the object in a cluttered
scene using two-stream convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) [31]. Furthermore, grasping an unknown object in a
International Journal of Mechanical & Mechatronics Engineering IJMME-IJENS Vol:20 No:04 51
201004-6161-IJMME-IJENS © August 2020 IJENS I J E N S
cluttered scene has been performed using CNN based on
point cloud with a single depth camera [32], depth sensor
[33], or three dimensional sensor [34][27] through difficult
environments due to occlusion between camera and objects.
Besides, understanding which off-policy of RL algorithms
are best suited for vision-based robotic grasping has been
studied in [35] based on the number of DRL methods such
as supervised learning (e.g. Q-learning, Monte Carlo,
Corrected Monte Carlo, deep deterministic policy gradient
(DDPG), path consistency learning (PCL), actor-critic
Algorithms, and double Q-learning (DQL)).
Deep Q-critic with a fully convolutional network (FCN)
has been implemented in grasping invisible object among
other objects [36]. Also, Q-learning with FCN framework
has been proposed for either robot picking task [37] based
on learning synergies from pushing and grasping policies,
or for pick-and-place task [18][38] using segmentation and
labelling of multiple views of a scene. Moreover, suction
grasp, as one of the common technologies for grasping in a
cluttered scene, has been executed using Q-learning with
ResNet and U-Net Structure [39], which are used to predict
picking region without recognition and pose estimation.
Training Q-learning with ResNet and U-net Structure has
been proven effective in solving grasping tasks without
pushing action. Other works, pushing polices has been
employed for singulation the target object, in which a sole
push policy is learned via Q-learning for the visible target in
clutter [16], whereas Deep Q-learning (DQN) has been
exploited to learn optimal push policies by trial-and-error
[40] in order to grasp the target object from its surrounding
clutter.
Recently, DRL methods have been effectively proven in
solving tasks such as inducing DQN for Object Grasping
using a Slide-to-Wall [41], soft Q-learning for object
placement task (e.g. stack Lego blocks together) [42], and
CNN policy research for grasping the object using stochastic
gradient descent [14]. Learning of Shifting objects, in such
a way that their grasp probability increases in Cluttered
Environments, has been performed using Q-learning with
FCN [43]. Rearranging objects on a tabletop surface has
also been done based on modeling the task with rewards and
training a deep Q-network [44][45]. Furthermore, a method,
which is called reinforcement learning with active queries
(RAQ), has been implemented to train a policy for placing
a book on the bookshelf and draping cloth [17][47].
With increase the challenges of manipulation tasks,
such as picking up the top of towels, which are folded and
stacked on a table, has been executed using Q-Learning with
Real-Time Object Detection (YOLO) [4]. They have aimed
to detect the part of stable manipulation. Moreover, learning
a CNN policy using a guided policy search (GPS) algorithm
has been employed to grasp sets of primitive shapes, where
the policy uses the information of vision sensor, robot
configuration, and desired grasping posture [47]. Besides,
challenging class of pick-place and re-grasping problems,
where the exact geometry of the objects to be handled is
unknown, has been solved based on collect n-Episodes of
experience before labeling the experience replay database
using the most recent neural network weights [48]. Whereas,
Marcus and Platt [49] have used hierarchical SE(3) sampling
(HSE3S) with the same purpose as in [48]. Lastly, reaching
and grasping objects has been executed based on training the
DNN, which maps raw image pixels to Q-values
corresponding to potential actions using the Q-learning
framework [50]. However, all the related aforementioned
works have been implemented using a complex framework,
which needs high GPU features to train their models, besides
the time training that is needed during the training tasks.
Here, we have made some comparative reviews for the close
related works to ours based on training resources as listed in

According to above Table 1, most of the related works are
concentrated on grasping action alone because they are
deeply focused on the pose estimation and the quality of grasp
besides grasping various types of objects with different
textures and shapes. Regarding datasets, some of the
aforementioned works used well labeled dataset [38] [28] that
either has been collected from the same work or from other’s.
Some of researchers used raw images, which are directly
captured by the camera, and then passed to model for further
manipulation. To this end, we noticed that most researchers
implemented complex architecture frameworks, which
require high features of GPU and high memory to speed up
the training process. In addition, they focused intensively on
executing primitive grasp action without taking into
consideration of where to place that object after grasping.
III. METHODOLOGY
A. Picking and Placing Framework
In our work, a camera captures RGB images of the scene,
and 3d point cloud information is used to generate
heightmaps at the robot workspace. The heightmap is rotated
by 36 different angles in order to generate a set of 36 pixel-
wise Q-value maps, thereafter passed into a grasping neural
network ( ), which is a fully convolutional DenseNet to
generate predictions of Q-values. Q-values are a measure of
future expected reward in the formula of Q-learning from
reinforcement learning [52]. Here they are visualized as a heat
map where hotter regions indicate higher Q-values. Each
pixel  represents a physical grasp centered at the point in the
scene oriented horizontally with respect to the heightmap. To
make predictions for different grasping orientations, we rotate
the height maps by 36 different angles before feeding it into
the network in order to generate a set of 36 pixel-wise Q-
value maps. This effectively gives us value predictions for 36
different grasping angles for every visible location at the
robot workspace. The grasping network () is trained
jointly as single Q-function, whereas Rewards are
automatically provided from successful grasps.
With reference to Figure 1, red cycle highlights the
highest Q-value map, which corresponds to the best grasp.
Rotating input height maps improve sample efficiency by
enabling the networks to share one set of learned features
across multiple different grasping orientations. In our
experiments, our model is able to successfully learn grasping
policies from scratch within 3000 trial-and-errors at 6
seconds per iteration.
The grasp FCN  has the network architecture
similar to that of [37][51]: that is, a DenseNet-121-pre-trained
on ImageNet, followed by 2 additional 1x1 convolutional
layers interleaved with the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and
Batch Normalization (BN) layers, then bilinearly upsampled.
The action that maximizes the Q-function is the primitive and
pixel with the highest Q-value across all 36 pixel-wise Q-
value maps:

B. Placing Task
As illustrated in Figure 1, once the robot has grasped an
object, placement action will be executed. The robot moves
to the place-workspace. Then the status of the gripper is
checked to ensure that the object is still in place. In the event
of slippage, placement action will be aborted. The robot then
returns to the home position for a new iteration.

Following [37] [51] , our FCN- is trained by
stochastic gradient descent (SGD) solver with momentum,
with a fixed learning rate of , momentum of 0.9 , and
weight decay of . To speed up the training process, the
model is trained with experience replay [53] using stochastic
rank-based prioritization, approximated with a power-law
distribution. The exploration parameter of ε-greedy is initially
set at 0.5, then annealed over training to 0.1. Future discount
is fixed at 0.2.
The model is trained by self-supervision with a
simulated tabletop environment. During training, 10 objects
are randomly selected from a basic block pool and dropped
into the 0.448×0.448 m2 workspace in front of the robot. By
trial-and-error, the robot then grasps and places the grasped
object at the 0.448×0.448 m2 place-workspace. The data
collection process continues until all objects have been
moved to the place-workspace, in which 10 objects are again
randomly dropped into the grasp-workspace.

IV. SIMULATION RESULT AND DISCUSSION
A simulation study has been conducted using V-REP. A
UR5 robot equipped with a parallel jaw gripper is used in the
study. The robot observes the environment via a fixed RGB-
D camera. The camera captures image and depth maps with a
pixel resolution of 640 x 480, where each pixel represents a
physical grasp centered at the point in the scene oriented
horizontally with respect to the heightmap. Upon reaching the
grasp position, both fingers attempt to move 4cm below
starting point (in the gravity direction) before closing the
finger. The grasp prediction network is built in PyTorch with
NVIDIA 1660Ti GPU on a 3.7GHz Intel Core i7-8700HQ
CPU.
A. Training Phase
During training, the robot performs the tasks of grasping
and placing 10 randomly selected objects over 3000 iterations
by trial-and-error. Two primitive actions are taken into
consideration, i.e., the robot picks up the object, and then
places it at the place-workspace. The training time taken for
each iteration varies between 6-12 seconds, depending on the
success of the grasp. For instance, once the robot fails to grasp
an object, the robot will not perform place primitive action,
and the agent needs about 6 seconds for one iteration. In
contrast, if the robot grasps an object successfully, the robot
will move to the place-workspace. At this point, the status of
the gripper will be checked to ensure that the object is still in
place; that is, the gripper is not fully closed if the object is
within the gripper’s fingers. Consequently, placement will be
executed. In this case, the robot will take about 15 seconds to
complete one iteration. In both cases, the robot returns to the
home position to start a new iteration. At this stage, we can
detect if the object delivers to place-workspace or not.
The robot records 2228 successful grasps out of 3000
trials, which is translated to the grasp efficiency and grasp
success rate of 77.4 and 74.3 %, respectively. On top of that,
place success rate of 98.42% has been achieved by the robot.
For illustration, the grasping performance versus training
trials is plotted in Figure 3. Grasping performance is
calculated by the percentage of grasp success rate for the most
recent m=200 grasp trials. At the earlier training trials, i.e.,
trials   , the number are scaled by 
.

all the 8 testing cases, where the number of objects are varied
from one test case to another as in Table 3, so this helps us to
clearly figure out the number of trials that are executed to
grasp the objects per completion repeatedly.
According to numerical analysis in Table 4, the grasping
success rate shows the ability of the policy to successfully
grasp objects. Overall, our framework achieves grasp success
rate of 80% or above across all 8 test cases. On top of that,
excellent grasp success rate above 90% has been recorded at
test cases 1, 3 and 8. On the other hand, grasp efficiency
measures the ability of the robot to grasp object within one
test run. Grasp efficiency between 80~88% has been attained
in test-case 2, 4, 5, and 6, and this increases to at least 90 %
through test-case 1, 3, 7, and 8 as indicated in Table 4.
As for the numerical analysis of place task, the place
success rate is conducted to measure the ability of the robot
to successfully place objects. In this part, we evaluated
placing object by taking the ratio of number of successful
place over the number of successful grasp. The purpose of
evaluation is to make sure that the object is successfully
placed at place-workspace through transition object after
robot has successfully grasped object. Overall, our
framework successfully placed objects with a place success
rate to at least 90 % through all test-cases as indicated in Table
4.

V. CONCLUSION
In many research studies that employ advanced robotic
techniques, the concern is mainly in achieving high accuracy
and precision such as in reaching and grasping tasks.
Recently, Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is used in
various robotic applications, particularly in robotic grasping.
Undoubtedly, grasping object is not an easy task and grasping
task also does not guarantee that the object will not slip once
placing action is executed. In this work, we have proposed a
complete manipulation system with an explicit framework.
We have presented our model based on DenseNet-FCN to
train Q-learning, which directly generates grasp poses from
RGB and depth images on a pixel-wise basis, instead of
sampling and classifying individuals grasp candidates like
other deep learning techniques.
Our proposed framework allows us to generate grasp
poses based on generating a set of 36 pixel-wise Q value
maps. This effectively gives us values for predictions of 36
different grasping angles for every visible location in the
robot workspace. We illustrate through grasping trials graph
that our manipulation system has the ability to acquire
learning in grasping objects through cluttered scenes.
Additionally, our pick-to-place framework can be trained
with less needed training resources such as GPU (6GB),
training time (15s per pick-to-place action). We evaluated our
system by using both sparse and cluttered scenes. Thus, our
framework achieved grasp success rate at almost more than
90% through test-case 1,3, and 8, and this decreases to be
between 80~88% in test-case 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Our framework
also performed grasping at grasp efficiency between 80~88%
in test-case 2, 4, 5, and 6, and this increases to at least 90 %
through test-case 1, 3, 7, and 8. As for place task, our
framework successfully placed objects with a place success
rate to at least 90 % through all test-cases.

Autonomous Grasping of Deformable Objects with Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Study on Spaghetti Manipulation
Article
Full-text available
  • Aug 2025
  • Gamolped Prem
  • Nattapat Koomklang
  • Abbe Mowshowitz
  • Eiji Hayashi
Packing food into lunch boxes requires the correct portion to be selected. Food items such as fried chicken, eggs, and sausages are straightforward to manipulate when packing. In contrast, deformable objects like spaghetti can give challenges to lunch box packing due to their fragility and tendency to break apart, and the fluctuating weight of noodles. Furthermore, achieving the correct amount is crucial for lunch box packing. This research focuses on self-learned grasping by a robotic arm to enable the ability to autonomously predict and grasp deformable objects, specifically spaghetti, to achieve the correct amount within specified ranges. We utilize deep reinforcement learning as the core learning. We developed a custom environment and policy network along a real-world scenario that was simplified as in a food factory, incorporating multi-sensors to observe the environment and pipeline to work with a real robotic arm. Through the study and experiments, our results show that the robot can grasp the spaghetti within the desired ranges, although occasional failures were caused by the nature of the deformable object. Addressing the problem under varying environmental conditions such as data augmentation can partially help model prediction. The study highlights the potential of combining deep learning with robotic manipulation for complex deformable object tasks, offering insight for applications in automated food handling and other industries.

Deep Reinforcement Learning Based Synergies Pushing and Grasping Policies in Cluttered Scene Using UR5 Robot
Article
Full-text available
  • Jun 2025
  • Birhanemeskel Alamir Shiferaw
  • Ramasamy Srinivasan
  • Tayachew Fikire
This paper presents deep reinforcement learning-based synergy between pushing and grasping systems to improve the grasping performance of the UR5 robot in a cluttered scene. In robotic manipulations, grasping an object in a clutter is fundamental yet a challenging activity for industrial applications. This is because numerous studies focused on improving grasping performance in cluttered environments using either a grasping-only policy or pushing and grasping without incorporating a pushing reward. Additionally, some research has been limited to using similar objects, such as cubes. This paper for mulated the mathematical modeling of the universal robot manipulator. The proposed model involves training two fully-connected convolutional neural networks that transfer visual observations of the scene to a dense pixel-wise sample of end-effector orientations and positions for each pushing and grasping action. A fixed RGB-D camera is used to take the raw images of the scene and generate a heightmap image. Before feeding the heightmap image to the fully convolutional network, it is rotated by 36 different angles to generate 36 pixel-wise Q-value predictions. Both pushing and grasping networks are self-supervised by trial and error from experience and are trained together in a deep Q-learning algorithm. Successful grasps have a reward of 1, while successful pushes have a 0.5 reward value. But unsuccessful actions have a reward of 0 value. The proposed policy learns pushing motions to improve future grasping in a cluttered scene. The experiment demonstrates that the proposed model can successfully grasp objects with an 87% grasp success rate while grasping only policy, no-reward for pushing policy, and stochastic gradient without momentum is 60%, 71%, and 79% respectively. Further, it has been demonstrated that the proposed model is capable of generalizing to randomly arranged cluttered objects, challenging arrangements, and novel objects.

Reinforcement learning for robot manipulation tasks in human-robot collaboration using the CQL/SAC algorithms
Article
Full-text available
  • Apr 2025
  • Anel Husaković
  • Lejla Banjanovic-Mehmedovic
  • A. Gurdić-Ribic
  • Isak Karabegović
The integration of human-robot collaboration (HRC) into industrial and service environments demands efficient and adaptive robotic systems capable of executing diverse tasks, including pick-and-place operations. This paper investigates the application of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Conservative Q-Learning (CQL)—two deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms—for the learning and optimization of pick-and-place actions within HRC scenarios. By leveraging SAC’s capability to balance exploration and exploitation, the robot autonomously learns to perform pick-and-place tasks while adapting to dynamic environments and human interactions. Moreover, the integration of CQL ensures more stable learning by mitigating Q-value overestimation, which proves particularly advantageous in offline and suboptimal data scenarios. The combined use of CQL and SAC enhances policy robustness, facilitating safer and more efficient decision-making in continually evolving environments. The proposed framework combines simulation-based training with transfer learning techniques, enabling seamless deployment in real-world environments. The critical challenge of trajectory completion is addressed through a meticulously designed reward function that promotes efficiency, precision, and safety. Experimental validation demonstrates a 100 % success rate in simulation and an 80 % success rate on real hardware, confirming the practical viability of the proposed model. This work underscores the pivotal role of DRL in enhancing the functionality of collaborative robotic systems, illustrating its applicability across a range of industrial environments.

Federated Learning-Based Framework to Improve the Operational Efficiency of an Articulated Robot Manufacturing Environment
Article
Full-text available
  • Apr 2025
  • Junyong So
  • In-Bae Lee
  • Sojung Kim
Although articulated robots with flexible automation systems are essential for implementing smart factories, their high initial investment costs make them difficult for small and medium-sized enterprises to implement. This study proposes a federated learning-based articulated robot control framework to improve the task completion of multiple articulated robots used in automated systems under limited computing resources. The proposed framework consists of two modules: (1) a federated learning module for the cooperative training of multiple joint robots on a part-picking task and (2) an articulated robot control module to balance the efficiency of limited resources. The proposed framework is applied to cases with different numbers of joint robots, and its performance is evaluated in terms of training completion time, resource share ratio, network traffic, and completion time of a picking task. Under the devised framework, the experiment demonstrates object recognition by three joint robots with an accuracy of approximately 80% at a minimum number of learning rounds of 76 and with a network traffic intensity of 2303.5 MB. As a result, this study contributes to the expansion of federated learning use for articulated robot control in limited environments, such as small and medium-sized enterprises.

Estimation of grasp type and determining grasping points for Adaptive Grasping Device

The article describes the grasping point algorithm (GPA), aimed to determine points for picking up objects by a manipulator equipped with a proprietary gripper enabling three picking modes (suction cup, two fingers, three fingers). The paper outlines the topic of unknown object picking using various types of grippers, both from a stack of objects and stand-alone items. It describes details of four methods available in the literature. Presented GPA algorithm consists of four separate functions dedicated to appropriate grasping methods chosen based on a decisionmaking process. The dedicated functions has been described in detail and tested. Used methods have been tested manually on 15 different objects. GPA algorithm has been evaluated in realworld tests as well. The presented tests showed efficiency of approximately 92% in the case of moving previously unknown objects from the stack to the target cuvette.

This paper introduces an innovative algorithm aimed at enhancing robot learning using dynamic trajectory modeling and time-dependent state analysis. By integrating reinforcement learning (RL) and trajectory planning, the proposed approach enhances the robot’s adaptability in diverse environments and tasks. The framework begins with a comprehensive analysis of the robot’s operational space, focusing on Cartesian coordinates and configuration systems. By modeling trajectories and states within these systems, the robot achieves sequential tracking of arbitrary states, facilitating efficient task execution in various scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate the algorithm’s efficacy in manipulation tasks and path planning in dynamic environments. By integrating dynamic trajectory modeling and time-dependent state analysis, the robot’s adaptability and performance improve significantly, enabling precise task execution in complex environments. This research contributes to advancing robot learning methodologies, particularly in human–robot interaction scenarios, promising applications in manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics.

  • Zhi Jin
Advances in sensor technologies have substantially reshaped human-machine interaction (HMI), enabling more intuitive, robust, and efficient interactions across diverse application domains including healthcare, robotics, and industrial automation. This review systematically covers next-generation sensing approaches essential to future HMI systems, addressing radar-based sensing, vision-based techniques, haptic feedback and teleoperation, as well as wearable sensors and wireless sensor networks (WSNs). Radar sensors are discussed for their reliability in challenging conditions and suitability for gesture and vital-sign monitoring. Vision-based sensors, incorporating monocular, stereo, near-infrared, and thermal imaging, provide detailed spatial and semantic information vital for gesture tracking and remote physiological monitoring. Moreover, haptic sensors and AI-driven teleoperation techniques are examined for their pivotal roles in enabling safe, precise remote interactions in medical and industrial contexts. This paper further explores IoT-enabled wearable sensors and WSNs, highlighting their application in continuous health monitoring and personalized healthcare. Sensor fusion strategies are discussed, emphasizing their potential to integrate complementary data streams effectively. Cross-cutting challenges such as computational efficiency, sensor integration, ethical considerations, and sustainability are identified and analyzed. By consolidating recent progress and discussing practical implementation issues, this review offers insights into current research trends and outlines key directions for future advancements in sensor-driven HMI systems.

Robotic Pushing and Grasping Knowledge Learning via Attention Deep Q-learning Network

August 2020 · Lecture Notes in Computer Science
  • Zipeng Yang
  • Huiliang Shang
Robotic grasping is a fundamental manipulation in multiple robotic tasks, which has great research significance. It is challenging to perform robotic grasping in cluttered environments due to the occlusion and stacking of objects. We propose an attention deep Q-learning network for robotic grasping with the assistance of pushing actions with non-sparse rewards. The attention network improves the ... [Show full abstract] performance of deep Q-learning network by weighting feature channels. The robot use pushing actions to dilute dense objects to create space for grasping. The pushing and grasping knowledge are learned by trial and error in a self-supervised way. To evaluate the robotic grasping performance, we present an overall performance metric, which contains three evaluation factors: task completion rate, grasping success rate and action efficiency. The experimental environment is established on the V-REP simulation software to verify our proposed model. The results show that our pushing strategy can not only improve robotic grasping performance but also avoid unnecessary pushing actions to improve action efficiency. At the same time, ablation studies prove the effectiveness of the attention mechanism. Our proposed method can achieve overall performance of 82.33% for robotic grasping.

Color Matching Based Approach for Robotic Grasping

July 2021
  • Marwan Mohammed
  • L.C. Kwek
  • Shing Chyi Chua
  • Esmail Ai Alandoli
Object grasping is a basic but difficult task in robotic manipulation due to various object size, shapes and other properties. The problem becomes more challenging when the robot has to reach for and grasp a particular object in cluttered environments. To this end, the color of object can be one of the important features for identifying the target object to be picked up. In this paper, we ... [Show full abstract] investigate an approach of training a robot so that it is able to locate the target object by matching its color, and goes on to pick up the object in an unsupervised learning manner. The proposed approach is divided into two parts: 1) a semantic segmentation module that locates the target object by segmenting the color image and creates a mask on the predicted target object, 2) an object pose estimation module that predicts the optimal grasp position of target object based on a deep reinforcement learning framework. The proposed approach was evaluated with various testing scenarios of handling single and multiple colored target objects. The experimental simulation results indicate that the suggested approach achieves an overall success rate of 92% in the grasping task.

Hyper‐Versatile Gripping: Synergizing Mechanical and Machine Intelligence of a Hybrid Robotic Grippe...

February 2024 · Advanced Intelligent Systems
  • Phone May Khin
  • Raye Chen-Hua Yeow
  • Marcelo H. Ang
Integration of robotic solutions in manufacturing sector is growing. However, it is still concentrated in certain industries (i.e., electronics and automotive) where standardization of product physical form is high. Current state‐of‐the‐art gripping solutions fall short when they need to accommodate items with high variability in physical form. This challenging scenario for automation can be ... [Show full abstract] found in a few industries (i.e., e‐commerce). Automation of pick‐and‐place processes in this area requires a more versatile gripping solution. To resolve this challenge, this article proposes a novel way to improve grip‐versatility by synergizing the mechanical and machine intelligence of a hybrid robotic gripper (HRG). Comparative analysis with commercial grippers shows that HRG can pick a more diverse range of items with success rate 94.78%. Visual perception‐based picking strategy is developed to automate the reconfiguration of HRG into a stable grasp pose for different objects. Using the proposed reconfigurable picking strategy, the efficacy of HRG in pick‐and‐place tasks is evaluated using three parameters—mean pick per hour (MPPH), successful execution over total attempts (SETA), and average cycle time (AVGCT). HRG can effectively pick items in cluttered workspace with MPPH of 98.54 ± 15.49, SETA of 0.93 ± 0.11, and AVGCT of 34.76 ± 3.31 s.
